series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm: swap: move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the insertion of a folio into the LRU (Least Recently Used) list out of the swap cache allocator function. The reason for this change is that zswap writeback requires a swap cache folio that can be freed directly once writeback completes, without being on the LRU. The patch introduces a new function __swap_cache_alloc_folio() that allocates a folio but does not add it to the LRU, allowing the caller to manage its lifecycle. This change is intended to be functional equivalent to the original code and only affects how the LRU is handled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm: swap: drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of swap cache folios by dropping them from their cache once writeback completes, rather than leaving them for reclaim to find later. This is achieved by adding a new function `swap_writeback_dropbehind_folio` that takes a folio as an argument and drops it from its cache after writeback has completed. The patch also updates several other functions to use this new function. The goal of the patch is to improve performance by reducing the number of times swap cache folios are scanned for reclaim, which can be expensive operations.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Barry Song expressed confusion about the patch's restriction to only support non-LRU folios, wondering if this limitation prevents potential optimizations for madv_pageout and noted that zram might benefit from the patch in the future.

Reviewer Barry Song noted that file-backed folios in other filesystems and drivers also use workqueues to handle dropbehind, and suggested extending the patch to include them for consistency.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Alexandre,
Thanks very much for your patch!

I don't quite understand why we only support NON-LRU folios. Does this
restriction prevent potential optimizations for madv_pageout?

Also, zram might benefit from your patch in the future with
asynchronous hardware compression and software compression such as
kcompressd[1].

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20250430082651.3152444-1-qun-wei.lin@mediatek.com/

[...]

---

This is good. For file dropbehind, I see both F2FS [1] and block
devices [2] reinventing workqueues in their own filesystems or
drivers, while folio_end_dropbehind() simply benefits from its safe,
sleepable context. This seems a bit odd.

So I'm really curious whether this could be extended to file-backed
folios as well, so that those filesystems and device drivers don't
have to deal with this themselves.

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260820071438.695893-1-qiwenjie@xiaomi.com/
[2] https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260730-blk-dontcache-v7-2-3e8e6850068d@columbia.edu/

Thanks
Barry

review_comments.author: Matthew Wilcox
review_comments.summary: The reviewer suggests basing the current patch on a different series by Tal, citing that it would be easier to implement
review_comments.raw_body:
You should probably both be aware of Tal's series:

https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260730-blk-dontcache-v7-0-3e8e6850068d@columbia.edu/

In fact, I'd base this series on Tal's.  It would be considerably
easier.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Barry Song pointed out that the question he asked in a previous email about how the swap cache folios are handled when writeback completes has not been addressed, and requested an answer to this question.

Reviewer Barry Song suggested using a bio_in_atomic() helper to determine if bio completion should be moved to a workqueue, and proposed reusing Tal's code for this purpose.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] mm: zswap: drop cold writeback folios via swap dropbehind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series optimizes zswap writeback by dropping cold folios from the swap cache after writeback completes, reducing unnecessary reclaim scans and memory residency.

review_comments.author: Sashiko
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about a potential race condition between swapoff and the dropbehind worker, which could lead to ghost anonymous folios being added to the LRU. Also pointed out that holding a reference to the folio until after __swap_writepage() returns could prevent the dropbehind optimization from working on fast or synchronous swap devices.

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary: Addressed Sashiko's concerns by explaining that the folio is marked dirty by folio_free_swap() itself, and that the resulting state is the same with and without this series. Also acknowledged the potential race condition but estimated it to be rare.
review_comments.raw_body:
I am pasting and answering Sashiko's review inline below.

On Tue, Aug 18, 2026 at 6:35 PM Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr> wrote:
>
> >
> zswap writeback decompresses an entry into a fresh swap cache folio and
> writes it back. The folio is cold by construction, yet it is left on the
> LRU for reclaim to find and free later, wasting a reclaim scan and keeping
> cold memory resident longer than necessary.
>
> Allocate the folio off the LRU and mark it PG_dropbehind so the swap
> dropbehind path frees it from the swap cache once writeback completes.
>
> Suggested-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>
> Suggested-by: Nhat Pham <nphamcs@gmail.com>
> Signed-off-by: Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr>
> ---
>  mm/zswap.c | 4 +---
>  1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 3 deletions(-)
>
> diff --git a/mm/zswap.c b/mm/zswap.c
> index 8163e6c5f76c..a35671e837f8 100644
> --- a/mm/zswap.c
> +++ b/mm/zswap.c
> @@ -1013,7 +1013,6 @@ static int zswap_writeback_entry(struct zswap_entry *entry,
>          */
>         if (IS_ERR(folio))
>                 return PTR_ERR(folio);
> -       folio_add_lru(folio);
>
>         /*
>          * folio is locked, and the swapcache is now secured against
> @@ -1046,8 +1045,7 @@ static int zswap_writeback_entry(struct zswap_entry *entry,
>         /* folio is up to date */
>         folio_mark_uptodate(folio);
>
> -       /* move it to the tail of the inactive list after end_writeback */
> -       folio_set_reclaim(folio);
> +       folio_set_dropbehind(folio);

Sashiko: "When setting dropbehind here, what happens if a concurrent swapoff
(try_to_unuse) removes the folio from the swap cache before the dropbehind
worker runs?
Looking at swap_dropbehind_drop_folio() in mm/swap_state.c:
if (folio_test_swapcache(folio) && !folio_test_writeback(folio) &&
remove_mapping(swap_address_space(folio->swap), folio, true, memcg)) {
dropped = true;
} else {
/* Raced: the folio is now owned by the swapin; put it back. */
folio_clear_dropbehind(folio);
folio_add_lru(folio);
}
If try_to_unuse() removes the folio from the swap cache, folio_test_swapcache()
will be false. The dropbehind worker will then blindly add the unmapped
anonymous folio to the LRU.
When reclaimed later, shrink_folio_list() will see it has PG_swapbacked but
no swap cache, causing it to allocate a new swap entry, mark it dirty, and
needlessly write the data back out to disk.
Could this race cause ghost anonymous folios to be added to the LRU?"

If swapoff frees the swap slot while the folio is queued for the dropbehind
drop, then yes, the worker takes the fallback and puts the folio back on the
LRU and that is exactly what has to happen: swapoff has just invalidated the
on-disk copy, so the folio now holds the only copy of the data. Leaving it off
the LRU would make it unreclaimable. Note the folio is marked dirty by
folio_free_swap() itself, for the same reason.

This is also not new: in the current code zswap's writeback folio is already on
the LRU when try_to_unuse() calls folio_free_swap() on it, so the resulting
state (unmapped, dirty, anon, on the LRU, no swap entry) is the same with and
without this series. Only the caller of folio_add_lru() differs.

>
>         /* start writeback */
>         __swap_writepage(folio, NULL);

Sashiko: "Does holding a reference to the folio until after
__swap_writepage() returns
prevent the dropbehind optimization from working on fast or synchronous swap
devices?
Because zswap_writeback_entry() holds a reference to the folio that isn't
released until it calls folio_put() at the end of the function, a race
can occur with synchronous I/O.
For synchronous devices (like zram), folio_end_writeback() is called and the
dropbehind worker is queued before __swap_writepage() even returns.
If the dropbehind worker calls remove_mapping() before zswap_writeback_entry()
calls folio_put(), remove_mapping() will see an unexpectedly high refcount
and fail.
The worker will then falsely assume a racing swapin and add the cold folio to
the LRU, defeating the purpose of the patch."

Yes, that race is real but I estimated it would be rare enough since
the folio_put() call is right after __swap_writepage(), and the time
the worker wakes up, the window is very small to me. I haven't
measured the actual rate, but I can measure it if needed. And if the
race is rare with sync devices, it is even more unlikely with async
devices.

In the end, I don't think any modifications are needed based on
Sashiko's review, let me know what you think.

Thanks,

Alex

> --
> 2.53.0-Meta
>
>

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series improves memory management for zswap by implementing a mechanism to promptly free cold writeback folios, reducing unnecessary reclaim scans and keeping cold memory resident for longer than necessary. The existing dropbehind mechanism is extended to swap cache folios, allowing zswap to opt into it. The patches move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator, drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion, and modify zswap to allocate its writeback folio off the LRU and mark it as dropbehind.

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where a swap cache folio is already on the LRU, and suggested adding a check to ensure it's not inserted into the LRU before being marked dropbehind.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti noted that a concurrent swapoff (try_to_unuse) can remove the folio from the swap cache before the dropbehind worker runs, causing the worker to blindly add the unmapped anonymous folio to the LRU. This can lead to ghost anonymous folios being added to the LRU when reclaimed later.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti noted that a race can occur between the dropbehind worker and zswap_writeback_entry() due to the folio reference being held until after __swap_writepage() returns, potentially causing remove_mapping() to fail if called before folio_put().

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/6] btrfs: use an on-stack path in btrfs_insert_orphan_item()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the btrfs_insert_orphan_item function to allocate a btrfs_path on the stack instead of dynamically allocating it, reducing the risk of memory allocation failures and transaction aborts. The change is motivated by the relatively small size of the btrfs_path structure (~112 bytes), making it feasible to allocate on the stack. This patch addresses an issue where a recoverable error could be turned into a transaction abort due to path allocation failure.

review_comments.author: David Sterba
review_comments.summary: Reviewer David Sterba expressed concerns about allocating a large btrfs_path on the stack, citing potential issues with stack consumption and allocation failures. He suggested arguing the trade-off in the changelog and exploring alternative solutions such as using __GFP_HIGH or reducing function parameters.
review_comments.raw_body:
112 is too much for on-stack, we've avoided that for btrfs_path in
particular, except some justified cases. This means in general the
beginning of call stack like ioctl, syscall handler and such. Otherwise
we assume there are other layers in the IO stack, like block device
drivers (DM), NFS, encoding layers or networking (iscsi), and obviously
the lowest level device drivers.

The trade off with possible allocation failure vs stack consumption
needs to be argued in the changelog, "is just 112" is not sufficient.

Getting back the consumed stack space is painful, we've been reducing
unneeded or redundant parameters of functions for years. The gains are
like -8 bytes here and -8 bytes there, allocation of +112 wipes that out.

If the place of allocation is critical we can consider that but we have
too many of them, anywhere during the transaction commit path or
irreversible metadata changes. Possibly using __GFP_HIGH could work, but
I haven't explored that.

Qu added the patches to for-next but I had no chance to look closely at
this patchset yet and am hesitant to leave it like that.

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged that the stack size is larger than initially assumed, but still justified the allocation failure leading to fs abort as acceptable given it's a GFP_NOFS allocation.
review_comments.raw_body:
Fair critique. These days I think we're mostly ~16k stacks, but it can
certainly get deep given the right layering.

In this case, failing this allocation can lead to aborting the fs, so
it seemed justified. This is a GFP_NOFS allocation too, so it can
easily fail, even though it's small.

Qu suggested this approach in an earlier review pass, so I'd be
interested to hear his take on this too.

Thanks for taking a look!
-- 
Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>

review_comments.author: Qu Wenruo
review_comments.summary:
reviewer pointed out inconsistency in on-stack memory usage between current patch and previous patches, specifically citing huge page support as an example where extra on-stack memory was allocated without hesitation, but is being hesitantly used in this patch; reviewer also questioned the 'deep-in-the-stack' argument and requested data to validate the impact of 112 bytes on on-stack memory usage

reviewer agreed with the patch but requested additional changelog information, specifically a good call trace to demonstrate the issue
review_comments.raw_body:
I think you're very inconsistent on on-stack memory usage at least.

You were fine when I was adding 128bytes for several call sites for the 
support of huge pages, and I'd argue all those call sites have a deeper 
stack, because it's on the writeback path.

Furthermore, that huge page support is not widely used, but everyone 
will need to pay that on-stack price.

On the other hand, you are also very hesitant on my recent patches 
removing those 128 bytes usages.

So your behavior doesn't seem to match what you said here.


Secondly, your deep-in-the-stack argument doesn't sound solid either.

Every block file system can be built upon layer of storage stacks, not 
only btrfs, but *every* block fs as long as there is a chance to do IO.
This means you're just saying, there can be almost-infinite lower layers 
under us, so we should not use any extra on-stack memory.

I do not think this is the sane nor really validated.

If you want to argue if the extra 112 bytes is good or not, give me some 
data about the on-stack memory usage.
With the proof that with enough stacked dm layer, that extra 112 bytes 
are going to cause problem.

Not to mention I believe some dm drivers are queuing the real submission 
handling into a workqueue, avoiding further increasing the on-stack 
memory usage.

---

Although I agree that more changelog will help, especially if Jeff has a 
good call trace showing that this is causing a flip RO in meta's fleet.

review_comments.author: Qu Wenruo
review_comments.summary: reviewer expressed concern about inconsistent on-stack memory usage and requested a consistent behavior
review_comments.raw_body:
For now I have removed those from for-next, but I really hope you can 
come up with a consistent behavior on on-stack memory usage.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/6] btrfs: use an on-stack path in btrfs_del_orphan_item()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the btrfs_del_orphan_item() function to allocate a path on the stack instead of dynamically, which reduces memory allocation failures that can cause transaction aborts. The change is made because the path is relatively small and only ~112 bytes in size, making it suitable for stack allocation. Additionally, the code is refactored to release the path via a common out label due to multiple exit points after the search.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/6] btrfs: split btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() into prealloc and commit phases
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() function into three separate functions: prealloc, commit, and free. The prealloc function allocates resources that can fail with -ENOMEM, while the commit function performs the actual insertion and cannot fail with -ENOMEM. This allows callers to return -ENOMEM cleanly without aborting the transaction. The original btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() is refactored into a thin wrapper that calls these new functions.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 4/6] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index before btree modification
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs file system to pre-allocate delayed directory index space before modifying the btree, preventing potential ENOMEM failures that could leave the btree in an inconsistent state. The allocation is now done in the btrfs_insert_dir_item function and can be optionally provided by the caller. The patch also removes a wrapper function for inserting delayed dir indices and updates various files to reflect these changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 5/6] btrfs: handle ENOMEM from btrfs_insert_dir_item() without aborting
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs file system to handle ENOMEM errors from btrfs_insert_dir_item() without aborting the transaction. It adds error handling for -ENOMEM in two functions, btrfs_add_link() and btrfs_create_new_inode(), allowing them to recover from memory pressure instead of crashing the filesystem. The patch also updates the orphan cleanup process to persist nlink 0 when an inode is orphaned due to ENOMEM. This change improves the robustness of Btrfs under memory-constrained conditions, preventing potential data loss and corruption.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 6/6] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index for non-overwrite rename
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to the Btrfs file system that allows pre-allocating delayed directory index resources before making any btree modifications during non-overwrite renames. This change helps prevent ENOMEM errors by ensuring that the necessary resources are available before attempting to modify the btree. The patch introduces a new function, `btrfs_prealloc_delayed_dir_index`, which is called in the `btrfs_rename` function when there is no overwrite target. If pre-allocation fails, an -ENOMEM error is returned immediately. For overwrite renames, the transaction still aborts on ENOMEM if earlier unlink operations have made irreversible btree modifications.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patchset addresses a long-standing issue in the Btrfs file system where memory allocation failures can cause an abort during synchronous directory operations. The patches rework the code to perform allocations upfront, before reaching the point of potential aborts. This approach is designed to work in conjunction with another series that aims to prevent new memory allocations from triggering ENOMEM errors. Although this patchset does not cover all possible cases where ENOMEM can occur, it provides a significant improvement over the current state and is intended as an intermediate step towards fully addressing the issue.

are going to cause problem.

Not to mention I believe some dm drivers are queuing the real submission 
handling into a workqueue, avoiding further increasing the on-stack 
memory usage.

---

Although I agree that more changelog will help, especially if Jeff has a 
good call trace showing that this is causing a flip RO in meta's fleet.
